title.rendered: From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)

content.rendered:
Rock and roll has a long tradition of dressing up tragedy in party clothes. From the rockabilly romp of “I Fought the Law” to the 21st-century alt-pop “Pumped Up Kicks,” rock musicians often wrap their bad news inside a boogie beat.

Few tracks in Bruce Springsteen’s catalog wear that mask quite as gleefully as “From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come).”

Recorded on Labor Day weekend during The River sessions and left on the cutting room floor for over two decades until The Essential Bruce Springsteen, “From Small Things” sounds on first listen like an unpretentious roadhouse rave-up.

It’s powered by a pumping Chuck Berry rhythm and a barreling barroom piano, but underneath lies a darkly comedic American crime chronicle about domestic entrapment, and an escalating spiral of small choices that ends in cold-blooded murder.

The song’s warning is right there in the title: Life rarely falls apart all at once; more often it unravels thread by thread, beginning with choices so mundane they barely register as crossroads. The song’s magic trick is Bruce’s ability to spin a full tragicomedy in just five brief stanzas.

At sixteen she quit high school to make a fortune in the Promised Land
She got a job behind the counter in an all-night hamburger stand
She wrote faithfully home to mama, “now mama don’t you worry none”
From small things, mama, big things one day come

Bruce opens by skewering one of his own favorite metaphors: the promised land. On his previous album, the phrase was an urgent, blowing-away-the-lies cry of defiance and determination. Here, our sixteen-year-old protagonist hits the highway chasing the same dream, only to wind up behind the counter of a greasy, all-night hamburger joint.

Yet notice her boundless youthful optimism. She writes home to assure her mother that flipping burgers on the graveyard shift is just a springboard to greater things. The chorus arrives here in its pure form: an article of sincere faith that humble beginnings inevitably bloom into fortune.

It was late one Friday, he pulled in out of the dark
He was tall and handsome, first she took his order then she took his heart
They bought a house on the hillside, where little feet soon would run
From small things, mama, big things one day come

Love arrives between orders. With impressive narrative economy, Bruce sketches a complete working-class courtship in four lines: a Friday night diner pickup, a sudden wedding, a modest house on a hillside, and a nursery full of children.

It’s the same scenario he explored solemnly in “The River.” But where that song examines the impact of youthful vows morphing into handcuffs though a long lens, here the pacing moves at cartoon speed. The small things of the first verse have yielded the big things of family and a mortgage. But there’s danger in moving too fast.

Oh but love is fleeting, it’s sad but true
When your heart is beating, you don’t wanna hear the news

The brief, philosophical bridge cuts to the chase: infatuation fades, but not before  common sense has long since flown out the window. For our heroine, domestic routine has curdled into suffocating boredom.

She packed her bags and with a Wyomie County real estate man
She ran down to Tampa in an El Dorado Grande
She wrote back, “dear mama, life is just heaven in the sun
From small things, mama, big things one day come”

Enter, stage right: a flashy real estate salesman driving an El Dorado Grande, with whom  Bruce’s protagonist makes her escape. She doesn’t just have a fling, she stages a wholesale jailbreak, trading the grey northern chill for sun-drenched Tampa.

(I’m assuming “down” means “south.” In an uncharacteristic move, Bruce sets his story in a county that appears to be entirely fictional. I can’t find a single Wyomie County anywhere in the United States.)

In her postcard home, the chorus takes on its first tinge of cynical irony. She thinks she has finally claimed her big things, confusing a convertible and a tan with true liberation.

But hold on: there’s a sudden plot twist ahead.

Well she shot him dead on a sunny Florida road
And when they caught her all she said was she couldn’t stand the way he drove

If this were a typical Springsteen ballad, we might get a reflective autopsy of the relationship’s demise. Instead, Bruce drops the guillotine in just two lines of deadpan farce.

Why did she pull the trigger on the highway in broad daylight? Not out of jealousy, it seems, or self-defense, or greed. She simply couldn’t stand the way he drove. It’s a comedic move that punctures the myth of a romantic outlaw flight before it even takes off.

But hey, whatever happened to her abandoned husband? Let’s check in on him.

Back home dear Johnny prays for his baby’s parole
He waits on the hillside where the Wyomie waters roll
At his feet and almost grown now, a blue-eyed daughter and a handsome son
Well from small things, mama, big things one day come

With a head-spinning pivot and fast forward, Bruce pulls the camera away from the Florida crime scene and pans to Wyomie County years later, where husband Johnny is raising two nearly grown children alone.

But Johnny isn’t bitter. In fact, he’s faithful to a fault, praying for a parole that almost certainly isn’t coming anytime soon. And in that final chorus delivery, the phrase reaches its final mutation. What started as an innocent teenage motto about ambition has yielded a broken home, a murder charge, two motherless kids, and a lifetime sentence.

Big things, indeed.

Musically, “From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)” is pure late-50s rockabilly funneled through the high-octane engine of the E Street Band. You can hear the hiccupping cadence of Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis’s percussive piano rolls, and Chuck Berry’s story-song precision.

Unfortunately, that vibe didn’t fit the narrative arc Bruce curated for The River. It would take almost a quarter-century before “From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)” received an official release on The Essential Bruce Springsteen.

Still, the song didn’t exactly stay locked away.

On May 30, 1981, Welsh rock-and-roller Dave Edmunds attended Springsteen’s concert at Wembley Arena, thanks to a DJ friend who scored them tickets and backstage passes, where Edmunds lingered after the show. “I was just standing there and someone tapped me on the shoulder and it was one of the crew,” Edmunds recalled.

“And he said, ‘Bruce wants to see you’ and I was whisked back to the dressing room. And Bruce said he had a song for me. He sang it on the spot, picked up the guitar and sang it…and it was perfect for me. ‘It’s yours, man!’ he said. A couple weeks later Bruce made a rough cassette – just guitar and vocal – and gave it to me.”

Edmunds took the song straight to the studio, covering the song for his next album and issuing it as its lead single. The song peaked at #28 on the Billboard Rock chart, introducing Bruce’s cautionary tale to an audience who had no idea he had written it.

Bruce may have given away his song, but he seemed to have taken a liking to it belatedly. No less than fourteen times in 1982 and 1983, Bruce jumped on Jersey Shore club stages to perform “From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come”)–including once with Edmunds himself.

When he finally broke it out live with the E Street Band late in the Rising Tour (and in rare outings in the years since), they delivered it with goofy grins befitting the song’s content.

“From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)” won’t be remembered as one of Bruce Springsteen’s finest songs, but it’s a great example of one of his under-appreciated talents as a master satirist of American restlessness. Few artists are capable of turning the dark downturn of a blue-collar dream into an irresistible rock and roll shuffle.

From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)
Recorded: September 2, 1979
Released: The Essential Bruce Springsteen (2003), The Ties That Bind: The River Collection (2015)
First performed: June 27, 1982 (Asbury Park, NJ)
Last performed: November 16, 2019 (Asbury Park, NJ)

jetpack-related-posts.title: Introduction: The River Beneath The River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: In the late fall of 2015, Bruce Springsteen released The Ties That Bind: The River Collection, a lavish celebratory retrospective of a classic double album. The package included such gems as a breathtaking, four-hour live concert film and the legendary, abandoned ten-track single album Bruce pulled back from the pressing…

jetpack-related-posts.title: Nitty Gritty Dirt Band: From Small Things (Big Things One Day Come)
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: "From Small Things" got some cover love long before Bruce officially released it. Here's one of the best. from the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band in 1990.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Angelyne
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: A cover that was almost a team-up in a parallel universe version of "The River" -- Gary U.S. Bonds and Steve Van Zandt replaced Bruce's original vocals on this outtake from the River recording sessions.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: Into the river we dive, as we appreciate one of Bruce's finest and most heartbreaking songs.

jetpack-related-posts.title: Johnny Bye Bye
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: An early rock and roll sequel and the tragic deaths of two of his musical heroes inspired this powerful, under-the-radar B-side.

jetpack-related-posts.title: The Clarks: The River
jetpack-related-posts.author: Ken
jetpack-related-posts.excerpt: The Clarks transform "The River" from ballad to full-on rocker, and it works--better than one might imagine was possible.
